newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-SERIOUS INJURY PROVES BLESSING IN DISGUISE.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SERIOUS INJURY PROVES BLESSING IN DISGUISE.

text.p: A serious skiing injury has proved a blessing in disguise for former British downhill champion David Cook.
Cook, 21, forced off the Alpine circuit by a chronic back injury, moved from two skis to four wheels and within two years had tested world champion Damon Hill's Williams car.
"It seems strange that just a few short years ago I wanted to compete in the Olympic Games in skiing but now I am putting everything into getting into Formula One," Cook said.
"I am still learning to run really in this sport and I don't want to go too fast too soon. Having seen what Damon Hill did as another late starter and late developer, I know that time is on my side."
Cook, who is also obsessed by snow boarding, has huge resources of determination, no fear of speed and a boundless ambition to reach the top.
"When I was skiing I wanted to do well on the slopes because I thought I was on the verge of doing better than either Martin or Graham Bell ever did," he said.

"The difference between them and me was that they wanted to be the best in Britain while I wanted to be the best in the world. I worked hard but then came the injury which devastasted me at the time."
Cook finds it galling to watch from the sidelines as some of his old rivals grab the headlines.
"When I watch some of best Swiss skiers winning downhills now, I remember beating them as a junior," he said.

"But you can't look back. I might not have been the best skier alive but I am certain I would have been the best in Britain. But it only makes me more determined to be successful in motor racing now."
Cook switched sports after winning the British downhill championship for four successive years from 1990 to 1993.
In 1995, in his first full season, he finished sixth in the British Formula Renault series before going on to win it this year.
The prize was a chance to try for Hill's cockpit for size and Cook liked the fit.
Cook's family is steeped in the sport.
His sister Paula, the youngest manager on the trading floor of the London Stock Exchange, races in British Formula Three for a team set up by their father Derek.
"I never expected to achieve quite this much so far but I like to think I am following Damon to the top because he started late in the sport as I have," Cook said.
"Like him, too, I have worked harder than anyone else in my discipline and so I am on a steep learning curve which I am confident will lead to a Formula One drive in the end."
Cook adapted quickly to the Renault-powered Williams.

"When I got into the car I was determined not to let the occasion get to me," he said. "I managed to keep my cool. I'm not overawed by it all and I know that I can drive a Formula One car as there's so much there to help the driver.
"At the end, despite going six seconds faster than I did at the start of the test, I still hadn't pushed for my maximum."
After the test the Williams team's long-serving test driver Bryan Lambert commented: "David conducted himself in a manner thoroughly befitting a professional racing driver.
"I will be reporting back to Frank Williams and I am sure we will be keeping an eye on him over the next season or two."
For now, Cook's ambitions are focused on Formula 3000 which he accepts will have to be his stepping-stone to the top.
"I know I can do well," he said. "After a couple of years in Formula Three I will be more than ready for Formula One."
